title: Coulomb Crystallization in Free Electron Beams
authors: Valerio Di Giulio, Rudolf Haindl, Armin Feist, Claus Ropers
abstract: Classical Coulomb crystals and quantum Wigner crystals typically arise when repulsive interactions order like-charged particles in spatially confined environments. Here, we show that transient crystallization can also emerge in freely propagating electron pulses without external trapping. Experimentally, we use a transmission electron microscope to measure number-resolved energy correlations in photoemitted pulses containing up to nine electrons, revealing strong correlations at small particle numbers that progressively disappear in the pulse interior as the number increases. To explain these observations, we combine many-body simulations with a one-dimensional statistical-mechanical model, showing that the leading and trailing electrons generate a self-induced longitudinal potential that transiently confines the inner particles, enabling the formation of an ordered chain during propagation. The resulting crystallization phase diagram reveals how many-body ordering dynamics can be understood in terms of evolving macroscopic beam properties, namely its geometry and the ratio of the mean Coulomb interaction energy to the longitudinal thermal energy. Extending this framework, we theoretically demonstrate that weak transverse guiding through electrostatic or optical ponderomotive forces can sustain crystallization at larger particle numbers and predict spontaneous longitudinal periodic bunching in continuous electron beams. Our results identify conditions under which stochastic Coulomb interactions can be harnessed to generate self-structured, strongly correlated electron beams in both pulsed and continuous regimes.
summary: This work demonstrates that electron beams can spontaneously form ordered Coulomb crystals in free space, driven by self-induced longitudinal potentials from the beam edges. By combining experiments with advanced 1D statistical models, the authors map out the conditions—including the role of weak transverse guiding—under which these strongly correlated, self-structured electron beams can be generated.
main_problem: The paper investigates the emergence of Coulomb crystallization in electron beams, specifically addressing how ordered phases can form in free space without external trapping fields.
main_result: Transient crystallization can occur in free electron pulses due to a self-induced longitudinal potential generated by the leading and trailing electrons, and weak transverse guiding can sustain this ordering for larger particle numbers.
method: The study combines experimental measurements of energy correlations with theoretical modeling using quasi-one-dimensional statistical mechanics and many-body simulations.
model_or_system: The system involves photoemitted electron pulses or continuous beams propagating through a vacuum. The physics is modeled using a quasi-1D approach with a softened Coulomb potential, incorporating self-consistent trapping potentials.
key_observables: Number-resolved energy correlations, mean-squared displacement ($\langle\delta z^2angle$), and the phase diagram mapping ordering dynamics against beam geometry and energy ratios.
important_parameters: Particle number ($N$), aspect ratio ($L/R$), and the ratio of mean Coulomb interaction energy to longitudinal thermal energy ($E_{	ext{Coul}}/E_{	ext{kin}}$).
main_assumptions: The 1D model assumes interactions are dominated by axial separations, and the self-trapping potential relies on the leading/trailing electrons providing confinement.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison between trapped and free-space Coulomb crystals, showing the geometry of self-confinement and the evolution of order parameters across different beam regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from observing transient crystallization in pulsed beams (small N) to developing a 1D statistical model explaining self-confinement, and finally extending the framework to predict sustained ordering in continuous beams using weak transverse guiding.
why_interesting: The concept of self-induced potential leading to structural ordering in a non-equilibrium, propagating beam is highly relevant to understanding collective behavior in quantum systems where external confinement is absent.
